name: Abijah (Rehoboam's son)
title: Judah's second king after the kingdom's division
summary: Abijah succeeded his father Rehoboam as the second king of Judah after the division of the united kingdom, and ruled for three years from Jerusalem. Son of Rehoboam and Maacah, he appears as a complex figure in the biblical sources. The Books of Chronicles depict his powerful defense speech for the Davidic dynasty and the legitimate temple service, delivered from Mount Zemaraim before a decisive battle against Jeroboam and the Northern Kingdom. Despite being heavily outnumbered, he won a convincing military victory and captured strategically important cities, including the cult center Bethel. The Books of Kings, however, paint a darker picture and state that his heart was not fully devoted to the Lord. Abijah is said to have taken fourteen wives and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters, which testifies to dynastic strength despite his short reign. His son Asa succeeded him on the throne.

keyEvents.title: Becomes king over Judah
keyEvents.description: Abijah was installed as king over Judah after his father Rehoboam's death and reigned for three years from Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Defense speech from Mount Zemaraim
keyEvents.description: Before the decisive battle, Abijah delivered a powerful exhortation from Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim. He defended the legitimacy of the Davidic dynasty and the lawful worship in Jerusalem, accusing Jeroboam of apostasy for setting up golden calves and dismissing the Levitical priests.

keyEvents.title: Victory over the Northern Kingdom
keyEvents.description: Despite Jeroboam's army of 800,000 men being twice as large as Abijah's 400,000, Judah prevailed because they relied on the Lord. According to Chronicles, 500,000 chosen men of Israel fell in this battle.

keyEvents.title: Conquest of Cities in the Northern Kingdom
keyEvents.description: After the military victory, Abijah captured several cities from Jeroboam, including Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron with their surrounding villages. The capture of Bethel was symbolically significant as it was one of Jeroboam's two cult centers with golden calves.

keyEvents.title: Abijah's Strength and Family
keyEvents.description: Abijah consolidated his power, took fourteen wives, and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. This demonstrates his dynastic strength during his short reign.

keyEvents.title: Death of Abijah and Asa's Accession to the Throne
keyEvents.description: Abijah died after three years of reign and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa succeeded him as king over Judah.

versions.summary: Abijah was the second king of Judah after the division of the kingdom, and the son of Rehoboam. He reigned for only three years but is known for his speech against Jeroboam, where he defended the house of David and legitimate worship in Jerusalem. Despite his short reign, he won a significant victory over Israel.

footnotes.text: The name Abijah (אֲבִיָּה) means 'my father is Yahweh' or 'Yahweh is my father,' expressing a theological confession. In 1 Kings, he is referred to as Abijam (אֲבִיָּם), possibly a deliberate change to avoid the theologically positive name Yahweh in connection with a king who received a negative evaluation.

The portrayal of Abijah varies significantly between Kings and Chronicles. In 1 Kings 15:3, it is said that 'his heart was not fully devoted to the Lord his God,' while Chronicles presents a much more positive account with his speech about faithfulness to Yahweh and his military victory. This difference reflects Chronicles' theological focus on temple service and the Davidic dynasty.

Abijah's mother is identified as 'Maacah, daughter of Absalom' in 2 Chron 11:20 and 1 Kgs 15:2, but as 'Micaiah, daughter of Uriel from Gibeah' in 2 Chron 13:2. Possible explanations include that Maacah/Micaiah are variant forms of the same name, or that 'daughter of Absalom' could mean 'descendant of Absalom' (grandchild through Uriel).

The figure of 500,000 fallen Israelites (2 Chron 13:17) is debated among scholars. The Hebrew word 'eleph' (אֶלֶף) can mean 'thousand,' but also 'military unit' or 'clan.' Some scholars believe the numbers should be read as military units rather than individual soldiers, which would yield more realistic casualty figures.

The capture of Bethel, mentioned in 2 Chron 13:19, is especially significant because Bethel was one of the two places where Jeroboam had placed the golden calves (1 Kgs 12:29). Abijah's conquest of this cult site underscores the theological dimension of the conflict between the two kingdoms.

Abijah's speech from Mount Zemaraim (2 Chron. 13:4–12) is a rare example of an exhortation speech ('Mahnrede') in the Old Testament, a literary form also found in other Old Testament texts and in ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions. The speech has a clear rhetorical structure with theological argumentation for the legitimacy of the Davidic dynasty.

The dating of Abijah's reign to approximately 913–911 BC is based on synchronization between the king lists of Israel and Judah. The exact chronology is debated, and scholars have proposed various models to harmonize the biblical numbers with each other and with external sources such as Egyptian and Assyrian annals.

Archaeological finds from the hill country of Judah dated to the 900s BC show a marked increase in settlements and fortifications during this period, which may correspond to the expansionist policy described under Rehoboam and Abijah. In particular, the fortifications mentioned in 2 Chron. 11:5–12 form the strategic background for Abijah's military operations against the north.
